title: React vs. Vue vs. Svelte: Which Frontend Framework Should You Pick in 2024?
note: Written for this revibe as a stand-in review article (not from the paper).

paragraphs.text: Choosing a frontend framework is one of the first decisions a web team makes, and one of the hardest to undo. We spent three weeks building the same dashboard application in React, Vue, and Svelte, then compared the experience on everything from bundle size to how long it took a new hire to ship a feature.

React remains the most widely used option by a wide margin, and that popularity pays off in practical ways. Almost every third-party widget, chart library, or authentication SDK ships a React binding first, and job boards are full of React postings. If your main concern is hiring or finding an answer on Stack Overflow at 2 a.m., React is hard to beat.

The learning curve, however, is steeper than it looks. JSX is easy, but hooks, memoization, and the rules around re-rendering trip up newcomers, and our junior developer spent two days chasing a stale-closure bug. React also does not include a router, a form library, or global state out of the box, so every team assembles its own stack, which makes projects look different from one another.

Performance was fine but unremarkable. Our React build weighed 142 KB gzipped, and the dashboard's large table noticeably stuttered until we added virtualization. React 18's concurrent features helped keep input responsive, but they required us to understand transitions and Suspense, which again raised the bar for the team.

Vue felt like the easiest of the three to pick up. Its single-file components keep template, logic, and styles together, and the official documentation is unusually clear. Our junior developer shipped her first feature in Vue in an afternoon, compared to most of a week in React.

Vue also comes with an official router and state library (Pinia), so the stack is more standardized across teams. The Composition API gives you React-style flexibility when you need it while the Options API remains available for simpler components. The bundle came in at 98 KB gzipped, and the large table rendered smoothly without extra work thanks to Vue's fine-grained reactivity.

The ecosystem is smaller than React's. Several commercial component libraries we wanted had no Vue version, and the pool of experienced Vue developers in our region was perhaps a third the size of the React pool. Vue is popular in Asia and Europe but has less enterprise adoption in North America, which may matter for long-term support.
Svelte: the newcomer with the best developer experience

Svelte compiles components to plain JavaScript at build time, so there is no virtual DOM and no runtime to ship. Our Svelte build was just 41 KB gzipped and the dashboard felt instant, with the large table scrolling at a steady 60 frames per second on a mid-range laptop.

Writing Svelte is a pleasure: components are mostly HTML with a sprinkle of reactive declarations, and there is far less boilerplate than in React. SvelteKit, the official application framework, handles routing, server-side rendering, and data loading with sensible defaults. Our whole team said Svelte was the most fun to write.

The trade-off is maturity. The ecosystem is young, some libraries lag behind, and the Svelte 5 release changed the reactivity model, which means tutorials from a year ago are already out of date. Hiring experienced Svelte developers is difficult, and we found fewer answers online when something went wrong. For a small team willing to read source code, this is manageable; for a large enterprise, it may be a risk.

Pick React if hiring, ecosystem breadth, and long-term corporate backing matter most, and accept a steeper learning curve and more decisions. Pick Vue if you want a gentle learning curve, good performance, and a standardized stack with official libraries. Pick Svelte if you prize raw performance and developer happiness and can live with a smaller, faster-moving community. Whatever you choose, the cost of the framework is dwarfed by the cost of switching later, so prototype a real feature before you commit.
